title: Create RDS and connect from EC2
goal: Goal: Create a private Amazon RDS for MySQL database, launch an EC2 client instance, allow access using security groups, and connect from EC2 to RDS.

concepts.title: RDS DB instance
concepts.body: Amazon RDS runs a managed relational database. You do not patch the database host yourself. You still control engine, size, storage, backups, and networking.

concepts.title: EC2 as database client
concepts.body: EC2 can act like an application server. The EC2 instance connects to the RDS endpoint. The database should usually stay private.

concepts.title: Private database design
concepts.body: RDS should normally be in private subnets. Do not make a database public unless there is a strong reason. Applications connect from inside the VPC.

consoleSteps.title: Create the EC2 security group

instructions.text: Open the EC2 console.
Choose Security Groups.
Choose Create security group.
Name it rds-task1-ec2-sg.
Select the default VPC.
Add inbound SSH 22 from your-ip/32.

Choose Security Groups.
Choose Create security group.
Name it rds-task1-db-sg.
Select the same default VPC.

Set the source to rds-task1-ec2-sg.

instructions.text: Open the EC2 console.
Choose Instances.
Choose Launch instances.
Name it saa-rds-task1-client.
Choose Amazon Linux.
Choose a small instance type such as t3.micro or t2.micro if available.
Place it in the default VPC.
Attach security group rds-task1-ec2-sg.
Launch the instance.

instructions.text: Open the Amazon RDS console.
Choose Databases.
Choose Create database.
Choose Standard create.
Choose MySQL.
Choose a low-cost template such as Free tier if available.
Set DB instance identifier to saa-rds-task1-mysql.
Set master username to adminuser.
Set a lab password and save it safely.

Set Public access to No.
Attach security group rds-task1-db-sg.
Create the database.

instructions.text: In the RDS console, open Databases.
Select saa-rds-task1-mysql.
Wait until status is Available.

consoleSteps.title: Connect to EC2 and install a MySQL client

instructions.text: Open the EC2 console.
Select saa-rds-task1-client.
Choose Connect.
Use EC2 Instance Connect or SSH.
Run sudo dnf install -y mariadb105 on Amazon Linux 2023.

instructions.text: On EC2, run mysql -h RDS-ENDPOINT -P 3306 -u adminuser -p.

VPC_ID=$(aws ec2 describe-vpcs --region $REGION --filters Name=is-default,Values=true --query 'Vpcs[0].VpcId' --output text)

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: a VPC ID like vpc-123456.

cliSteps.title: Create security groups

commands.text:
EC2_SG_ID=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --region $REGION --group-name $EC2_SG_NAME --description 'EC2 client security group for RDS task 1' --vpc-id $VPC_ID --query 'GroupId' --output text)
DB_SG_ID=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --region $REGION --group-name $DB_SG_NAME --description 'RDS DB security group for task 1' --vpc-id $VPC_ID --query 'GroupId' --output text)

echo $DB_SG_ID

commands.text:
MY_IP=$(curl -s https://checkip.amazonaws.com)/32
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --region $REGION --group-id $EC2_SG_ID --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr $MY_IP
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --region $REGION --group-id $DB_SG_ID --protocol tcp --port 3306 --source-group $EC2_SG_ID

cliSteps.warning: The curl command uses an internet service to find your public IP.

SUBNETS=$(aws ec2 describe-subnets --region $REGION --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC_ID --query 'Subnets[0:2].SubnetId' --output text)

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: RDS accepts at least two subnets.

cliSteps.title: Create the RDS DB instance

commands.text:
read -s -p 'Enter a temporary DB password: ' DB_PASS
echo

echo $DB_ENDPOINT

cheatSheet.title: RDS basic rule
cheatSheet.body: RDS = managed relational database. RDS manages the database host. You manage schema, users, and app access.

cheatSheet.title: RDS endpoint
cheatSheet.body: RDS endpoint = DNS name for the database. Applications connect to the endpoint. Do not connect to an RDS instance ID.

cheatSheet.title: Private database
cheatSheet.body: RDS private = no public internet access. EC2 in the VPC can still connect. This is the normal exam design.

cheatSheet.title: Security group source
cheatSheet.body: RDS SG should allow the EC2 SG. Do not use broad CIDRs for app access. Security group references are cleaner.

cheatSheet.title: MySQL port
cheatSheet.body: MySQL uses port 3306. PostgreSQL uses 5432. SQL Server often uses 1433.

cheatSheet.title: DB subnet group
cheatSheet.body: DB subnet group = subnets RDS can use. RDS needs subnet placement. Multi-AZ needs more than one AZ.

cheatSheet.title: Public access trap
cheatSheet.body: Publicly accessible = reachable from the internet path. It still needs security group access. Best answer is usually private DB.

cheatSheet.title: EC2 client pattern
cheatSheet.body: EC2 app server connects to RDS. EC2 SG is the allowed source. RDS SG protects the database.

cheatSheet.title: Connection failure memory
cheatSheet.body: Failure can be DNS, route, SG, NACL, credentials, or engine status. Check network first. Then check login details.

cheatSheet.title: RDS availability
cheatSheet.body: RDS must be available before connection. Creating can take minutes. Endpoint appears before it is usable.

cheatSheet.title: Credentials
cheatSheet.body: RDS master password is not IAM by default. Database users are separate from IAM users. IAM database authentication is optional.

cheatSheet.title: Cost memory
cheatSheet.body: RDS costs while running. Storage costs also apply. Final snapshots can cost money.

cheatSheet.title: Cleanup order
cheatSheet.body: Delete EC2 first. Delete RDS next. Delete subnet group and security groups last.

cheatSheet.title: Exam decision
cheatSheet.body: Need managed SQL database = RDS. Need serverless relational = Aurora Serverless. Need NoSQL key-value = DynamoDB.

troubleshooting.title: AccessDenied
troubleshooting.body: Check Console step 0 permissions. Run aws sts get-caller-identity. Confirm you are using the expected account.

troubleshooting.title: DB not available
troubleshooting.body: Wait until RDS status is available. Do not test while the DB is creating or modifying.

troubleshooting.title: Connection times out
troubleshooting.body: Check the RDS security group. Allow port 3306 from the EC2 security group. Check NACLs if changed.

troubleshooting.title: Access denied for user
troubleshooting.body: The network works, but database login failed. Check username and password. Check the DB engine user.

troubleshooting.title: Unknown host
troubleshooting.body: Check the copied RDS endpoint. Do not include https://. Use the endpoint DNS name only.

troubleshooting.title: Security group delete fails
troubleshooting.body: A resource still uses the security group. Delete the EC2 instance or RDS DB first. Then delete the security group.

examTraps.title: Trap 1 — Public RDS
examTraps.body: Wrong idea: make RDS public so EC2 can connect. Correct idea: keep RDS private and allow EC2 security group access.

examTraps.title: Trap 2 — IAM vs DB login
examTraps.body: Wrong idea: IAM user password logs into MySQL. Correct idea: database users are separate unless IAM DB auth is enabled.

examTraps.title: Trap 3 — Endpoint confusion
examTraps.body: Wrong idea: connect to the DB identifier. Correct idea: connect to the RDS endpoint DNS name.

examTraps.title: Trap 4 — Security group direction
examTraps.body: Wrong idea: only configure EC2 inbound. Correct idea: RDS inbound must allow the DB port from EC2.

examTraps.title: Trap 5 — Subnet group
examTraps.body: Wrong idea: RDS needs one subnet only. Correct idea: DB subnet groups normally span multiple AZs.

examTraps.title: Trap 6 — Multi-AZ read scaling
examTraps.body: Wrong idea: Multi-AZ gives read scaling. Correct idea: Multi-AZ is mainly high availability.

title: Create a Multi-AZ RDS database
goal: Goal: Create an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance, understand the standby instance, trigger a controlled failover, and verify the endpoint still stays the same.

concepts.title: Multi-AZ DB instance
concepts.body: Amazon RDS Multi-AZ creates a standby copy in another Availability Zone. The standby is for high availability. It is not used for normal read traffic.

concepts.title: Failover
concepts.body: Failover means RDS promotes the standby database. The database endpoint stays the same. Your application normally reconnects to the same endpoint.

concepts.title: Multi-AZ is not read scaling
concepts.body: Multi-AZ DB instance = availability. Read Replica = read scaling. Do not choose Multi-AZ when the exam asks for more read capacity.

cheatSheet.title: Standby database
cheatSheet.body: Standby = kept in another Availability Zone. Standby = managed by AWS. Standby = promoted during failover.

cheatSheet.title: Endpoint rule
cheatSheet.body: RDS endpoint = application connection name. Failover changes the primary behind the endpoint. The app should reconnect to the same endpoint.

cheatSheet.title: Read scaling trap
cheatSheet.body: Read scaling needed = choose Read Replica. High availability needed = choose Multi-AZ. Global read locality = consider cross-Region replica or Aurora Global Database.

cheatSheet.title: Backup benefit
cheatSheet.body: Multi-AZ can reduce backup impact. RDS may use the standby for some maintenance operations. Backups still need retention settings.

cheatSheet.title: Failover causes interruption
cheatSheet.body: Failover is not zero downtime. Connections can drop. Applications need retry logic.

cheatSheet.title: Common failover triggers
cheatSheet.body: AZ outage can trigger failover. DB instance failure can trigger failover. Planned maintenance can trigger failover. Manual reboot with failover can test it.

cheatSheet.title: Single standby vs DB cluster
cheatSheet.body: Multi-AZ DB instance = one standby. Multi-AZ DB cluster = two readable standbys for supported engines. Know which design the question describes.

cheatSheet.title: Cost memory
cheatSheet.body: Multi-AZ costs more than Single-AZ. You pay for standby capacity and storage. Use it when availability matters.

cheatSheet.title: Security group memory
cheatSheet.body: RDS security group should allow only the app source. Do not open MySQL to 0.0.0.0/0. Use security group referencing where possible.

cheatSheet.title: Subnet group memory
cheatSheet.body: RDS subnet group = subnets RDS can use. Multi-AZ needs more than one AZ. Private subnets are normal for databases.

cheatSheet.title: Troubleshooting memory
cheatSheet.body: Connection timeout = route or security group issue. Access denied = database username or password issue. Endpoint not found = DB still creating or wrong Region.

cheatSheet.title: Cleanup memory
cheatSheet.body: Delete EC2 first. Delete RDS next. Delete subnet group after RDS is gone. Delete security groups last.

cheatSheet.title: Car listening phrase
cheatSheet.body: Multi-AZ means survive an AZ. Read Replica means scale reads. Endpoint stays the app target.

troubleshooting.title: DB creation is slow
troubleshooting.body: RDS database creation can take several minutes. Multi-AZ usually takes longer than Single-AZ.

troubleshooting.title: Cannot connect from EC2
troubleshooting.body: Check the RDS security group. Allow port 3306 from the EC2 client security group. Do not use your laptop IP if the database is private.

troubleshooting.title: DB endpoint does not work
troubleshooting.body: Confirm the DB status is Available. Confirm you copied the endpoint, not the DB identifier. Confirm the port is 3306.

troubleshooting.title: Access denied in MySQL
troubleshooting.body: This usually means the username, password, or database user grants are wrong. It is different from a network timeout.

troubleshooting.title: Failover option not visible
troubleshooting.body: Confirm the DB is Multi-AZ. Single-AZ instances do not have standby failover. Some console wording can differ by engine.

troubleshooting.title: Security group will not delete
troubleshooting.body: Delete the RDS DB first. Wait until RDS is fully deleted. Then delete the security group.

examTraps.title: Trap 1 — Multi-AZ is not Read Replica
examTraps.body: Wrong choice: Multi-AZ for read scaling. Correct idea: Multi-AZ is mainly for high availability and failover.

examTraps.title: Trap 2 — standby is not normally readable
examTraps.body: Wrong choice: send reports to the standby. Correct idea: use a Read Replica for normal reporting reads.

examTraps.title: Trap 3 — endpoint should not be hardcoded to an IP
examTraps.body: Wrong choice: connect to the DB instance IP. Correct idea: connect to the RDS endpoint DNS name.

examTraps.title: Trap 4 — failover is not zero downtime
examTraps.body: Wrong choice: assume no dropped connections. Correct idea: applications need retry and reconnect logic.

examTraps.title: Trap 5 — Multi-AZ is not multi-Region
examTraps.body: Wrong choice: Multi-AZ for regional disaster recovery. Correct idea: use cross-Region designs for Region failure planning.

examTraps.title: Trap 6 — public access is not needed
examTraps.body: Wrong choice: make the database public for EC2 access. Correct idea: keep RDS private and allow EC2 security group access.

title: Take an RDS snapshot and restore a new database

concepts.title: RDS manual snapshot
concepts.body: A manual snapshot is a backup you create yourself. It stays until you delete it.

concepts.title: Snapshot restore creates a new DB
concepts.body: Restoring an RDS snapshot creates a new DB instance. It does not overwrite the old DB instance.

concepts.title: Snapshot scope
concepts.body: An RDS DB snapshot backs up the whole DB instance storage, not just one table.

concepts.title: IAM permissions needed

concepts.title: Encryption at Rest

concepts.title: AWS KMS (Key Management Service)

whyItMatters: Data security and corporate compliance mandates routinely demand encryption at rest. Knowing how and when to enable KMS handles a core piece of data security engineering on the AWS exams.

title: Compare RDS Backup, Snapshot, and PITR
goal: Goal: Configure automated backups, take a manual snapshot, and explore Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) mechanisms to understand RDS data protection.

concepts.title: Automated Backups & PITR
concepts.body: RDS uploads daily storage volume backups and continuously archives transaction logs (write-ahead logs) to S3. This combo enables Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) down to a specific second.

concepts.title: Manual DB Snapshots
concepts.body: User-initiated storage volume backups that are retained indefinitely, even after you delete the parent RDS database instance. They never expire automatically.

whyItMatters: Architecting for disaster recovery requires knowing the trade-offs between automated retention vs. manual persistence. The exam heavily tests RPO/RTO scenarios using these three features.

cheatSheet.title: Automated Backup Lifecycle
cheatSheet.body: Automated backups delete automatically when you delete the parent RDS instance. Retention spans from 1 to 35 days. Setting retention to 0 completely disables automated backups and purges PITR history logs.

cheatSheet.title: Manual Snapshot Longevity
cheatSheet.body: Manual snapshots survive database deletion entirely. They remain on AWS storage until you manually log in and delete them.

cheatSheet.title: Point-in-Time Recovery Mechanics
cheatSheet.body: PITR references your daily automated backup image + incremental transaction logs to reconstruct an identical instance clone at any given target second within your retention bracket.

troubleshooting.title: Missing Restore Options
troubleshooting.body: Cause: Automated backup tracking was disabled (retention period set to 0). Fix: Modify your database properties, change backup retention settings to at least 1 day, and wait for a new backup routine to initialize.

troubleshooting.title: Snapshot Status Blocked
troubleshooting.body: Cause: Attempting to create a snapshot while the parent DB is undergoing hardware modifications or heavy software upgrades. Fix: Wait until the core RDS resource state shifts back to 'Available' before initiating a backup call.

examTraps.title: The Overwrite Trap
examTraps.body: Exam questions might suggest that executing PITR or restoring an RDS snapshot overwrites the existing live production database. This is false. Restoring *always* spins up a completely separate database with a new endpoint string.

examTraps.title: Instance Deletion Backup Purge
examTraps.body: Be careful: if a question states an instance was terminated and asks how to recover data from an *automated* backup, you can't—unless you specifically checked the box to retain automated backups during deletion. Manual snapshots are the only ones preserved by default.

memoryHook: Automated dies with the instance; Manual lives on. Automated backups match the DB instance's lifespan. Manual snapshots stay until *you* say goodbye.

title: Create an Amazon Aurora Cluster
goal: Goal: Provision an Amazon Aurora relational database cluster featuring a shared storage architecture with a primary writer instance and a reader instance.

concepts.title: Shared Storage Architecture
concepts.body: Unlike traditional RDS, Aurora separates compute from storage. It maintains 6 copies of your data across 3 Availability Zones automatically, backed by a single shared cluster volume.

concepts.title: Cluster vs. Instance Endpoints
concepts.body: Aurora exposes a single Cluster Endpoint (Writer) for inserts/updates and a Reader Endpoint that load-balances read-only traffic automatically across all replicas.

whyItMatters: Aurora is AWS's flagship enterprise cloud-native database. Knowing how it delivers high performance, self-healing storage, and rapid failovers is a critical theme across modern AWS architectural design questions.
costWarning: Aurora cluster, database instance, storage, I/O, and backup charges apply. Complete cleanup promptly after testing.

cheatSheet.title: Aurora Scaling Limits
cheatSheet.body: An Aurora cluster can scale out up to 15 low-latency reader replicas to handle intense application read-query operations.

cheatSheet.title: Storage Auto-Scaling
cheatSheet.body: Aurora handles storage dynamically. It allocates blocks in 10 GB increments up to a total storage footprint boundary of 128 TiB without manual administrative manual overrides.

troubleshooting.title: Engine Version Mismatches
troubleshooting.body: Cause: Specifying an out-of-date or region-restricted version tag via the AWS CLI query execution format. Fix: Omit the explicit engine version attribute to automatically pull down the default stable image recommendation.

troubleshooting.title: Subnet Group Configuration Requirements
troubleshooting.body: Cause: Your default cluster network structure lack routes crossing multiple geographical boundaries. Fix: Ensure your target standard DB Subnet Group includes mapping IDs spanning at least two distinctive active regional Availability Zones.

examTraps.title: The Shared Storage Fallacy
examTraps.body: The exam might trick you into thinking each Aurora read replica requires manual replication replication sync configuration or separate storage pricing provisioning. Remember: all instances within an Aurora cluster attach to the same shared, single virtual storage volume layer.

examTraps.title: Endpoint Connection Swaps
examTraps.body: Do not hardcode specific instance node strings into your applications. If a failover occurs, a reader promotes to a writer. Hardcoding instance endpoints breaks updates. Always connect using the master Cluster Endpoint for writes.

title: Configure Aurora Replicas and Endpoints
goal: Goal: Scale an existing Amazon Aurora database cluster by adding a secondary reader replica, and examine how application traffic splits using specialized writer and reader endpoints.

concepts.title: Cluster Endpoint (Writer)
concepts.body: A dynamic DNS entry that pointing directly to the primary DB instance. It handles all write traffic (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE). If the primary instance fails, this endpoint updates instantly to point to the newly promoted master.

concepts.title: Reader Endpoint
concepts.body: A single DNS string that automatically load-balances incoming read requests (SELECT statements) across all available Aurora read replicas in the cluster.

whyItMatters: Separating read queries from write modifications ensures operational stability during sudden application traffic spikes. Configuring application pools to target distinct database endpoints is a baseline pattern for passing AWS architectural questions.

cheatSheet.title: Endpoint Abstract DNS Advantages
cheatSheet.body: Using abstract cluster endpoint connections keeps your application free from hardcoded instance references. When a server goes down or rolls over, the virtual endpoint updates behind the scenes to keep your app running smoothly.

cheatSheet.title: Reader Load Balancing Mechanics
cheatSheet.body: The Reader Endpoint alternates connections across your entire fleet of replica nodes using a basic round-robin DNS pattern. For advanced or heavy connection management, use custom target proxy mechanisms.

troubleshooting.title: Stale DNS Cache Errors
troubleshooting.body: Cause: Local application runtime code or client setups cache the underlying IP addresses of endpoint records too tightly during a failover sequence. Fix: Adjust your database connection pool properties to use a low Time-To-Live (TTL) value of less than 30 seconds.

troubleshooting.title: Replica Lag Violations
troubleshooting.body: Cause: Extreme mass transaction bursts on the primary writer node outrun the underlying storage engine synchronization context speeds. Fix: Scale up compute specs to match node sizing options, or check your local thread pool saturation levels.

examTraps.title: Hardcoding Node Endpoints
examTraps.body: Watch out for scenario options that recommend connecting application servers to the individual backend compute node names (e.g., instance-1.xxxx.region.rds.amazonaws.com). If a failover occurs, that node will change roles or reboot, causing write operations to fail. Always connect using the top-level Cluster Endpoint for writes.

examTips.text: SAA-C03: Master Amazon Aurora concepts and multi-AZ / replication design in Amazon Aurora.

memoryHook: Writers take edits; Readers share queries. The Writer endpoint routes data modifications to the master node, while the Reader endpoint automatically distributes read queries across your replica fleet.

title: Compare Aurora Serverless vs provisioned Aurora
goal: Goal: Compare Aurora Serverless v2 and provisioned Aurora so you know when each one is the better database choice.

concepts.title: Aurora cluster
concepts.body: An Aurora cluster has shared storage and one or more DB instances. The storage is separate from the compute.

concepts.title: Provisioned Aurora
concepts.body: Provisioned Aurora uses fixed DB instance classes, such as db.r6g.large. You choose the size before the database runs.

concepts.title: Aurora Serverless v2
concepts.body: Aurora Serverless v2 uses Aurora Capacity Units, also called ACUs. It scales database compute up and down inside the range you choose.

concepts.title: ACU
concepts.body: An ACU is a unit of Aurora Serverless capacity. Each ACU includes memory, CPU, and networking capacity.

concepts.title: IAM permissions needed
concepts.body: For this comparison lab, you need permission to view RDS and Aurora settings. For a personal lab account, an admin user is okay. In a company, use least privilege.

whyItMatters: AWS exams often ask you to choose between steady predictable database capacity and automatic scaling for changing database demand.

concepts.title: Amazon Aurora Overview

consoleSteps.title: Evaluate Data Model and Schema Flexibility

instructions.text: Use Amazon RDS or Aurora when your application requires complex SQL queries, multi-table `JOIN` operations, or strict relational ACID compliance.
Use Amazon DynamoDB when your application requires flexible JSON schemas, simple key-value lookups, or document storage without relational constraints.

consoleSteps.note: DynamoDB does not support native multi-table SQL JOIN operations.

consoleSteps.title: Evaluate Scaling and Latency Requirements

instructions.text: Use DynamoDB when read/write latency MUST remain under 10 milliseconds regardless of data volume or traffic growth.
Use Aurora when you need maximum relational SQL throughput (up to 15 Read Replicas with sub-10ms replication lag).
Use RDS for standard corporate relational database engines requiring moderate scaling.

consoleSteps.note: DynamoDB scales horizontally automatically across SSD partitions.

consoleSteps.title: Evaluate Multi-Region Availability Strategy

instructions.text: Choose DynamoDB Global Tables for multi-Region Active-Active read/write capabilities.
Choose Aurora Global Database for multi-Region Active-Passive relational disaster recovery (< 1 second cross-region replication lag).
Choose RDS Cross-Region Replicas for standard asynchronous relational backup read replicas.

consoleSteps.note: Global Tables provide active multi-Region writing; Aurora Global Database provides single-writer multi-region reads.

consoleSteps.title: Evaluate High Availability and Storage Architecture

instructions.text: Review Aurora 6-way replication: Aurora replicates data 6 ways across 3 Availability Zones, tolerating loss of 2 copies without affecting write availability.
Review RDS Multi-AZ: Synchronous physical EBS block replication to a standby instance in a second Availability Zone.
Review DynamoDB Multi-AZ: Built-in multi-AZ synchronous storage replication.

consoleSteps.note: Aurora's storage engine is decoupled from compute nodes.

cheatSheet.title: Partition Key (HASH)
cheatSheet.body: Single primary key value hashed by DynamoDB to distribute items across physical SSD storage partitions.

cheatSheet.title: Schema Flexibility
cheatSheet.body: Only primary key attributes are required during table creation. Items can store any number of unique attributes.

cheatSheet.title: GetItem vs Scan

title: Add a Sort Key & Query DynamoDB Data
goal: Goal: Create a table with a Composite Primary Key (Partition Key + Sort Key), load item collections, and run Query vs. Scan operations using comparison operators on the sort key.

concepts.title: Composite Primary Key (PK + SK)
concepts.body: Combines a Partition Key (PK) and Sort Key (SK). Items sharing the same PK form an Item Collection sorted physically by SK.

concepts.title: Query Operation
concepts.body: Finds items matching a specific Partition Key and optionally filters by Sort Key conditions (e.g. OrderDate >= 2026-03-01). Highly efficient and low RCU.

concepts.title: Scan Operation
concepts.body: Reads every item in the entire table sequentially. Consumes high RCU throughput, scales poorly, and should be avoided in production.

concepts.title: Sort Key Comparison Operators
concepts.body: DynamoDB Queries support begins_with, between, >, , >=, and on Sort Key values.

concepts.title: Query vs Scan Comparison Decision Matrix
concepts.body: OperationTarget ScopeRCU ConsumptionPerformanceSAA-C03 RecommendationQuerySingle Partition Key (Item Collection)Low (Only matches read)Fast (Primary choice for application lookupsScanEntire Table (All Partitions)High (Evaluates all items)Slow (Linear degradation)Avoid except for small maintenance audits

whyItMatters: This matters because the difference between inefficient table-wide Scan calls and efficient targeted Query operations is heavily tested on SAA-C03.

title: Configure DynamoDB On-Demand vs Provisioned Capacity
goal: Goal: Switch table capacity modes between Provisioned (setting Read/Write Capacity Units - RCUs/WCUs with Auto Scaling) and On-Demand capacity modes.

concepts.title: Provisioned Capacity Mode
concepts.body: Specify fixed Read Capacity Units (RCUs) and Write Capacity Units (WCUs). Best for predictable traffic; supports Auto Scaling and Reserved Capacity discounts.

concepts.title: On-Demand Capacity Mode (PAY_PER_REQUEST)
concepts.body: Instantly accommodates spiky, unpredictable workloads without capacity planning. Pay only per read/write request.

concepts.title: Read Capacity Unit (RCU)
concepts.body: 1 RCU = 1 strongly consistent read/sec (or 2 eventually consistent reads/sec) for items up to 4 KB.

concepts.title: Write Capacity Unit (WCU)
concepts.body: 1 WCU = 1 write/sec for items up to 1 KB.

concepts.title: Provisioned vs On-Demand Capacity Decision Matrix
concepts.body: FeatureProvisioned Capacity ModeOn-Demand Capacity ModeWorkload typePredictable, steady-state continuous trafficUnpredictable, spiky, or brand-new workloadsCapacity planningRequired (Specify RCUs & WCUs)None required (Instant auto-scale)Billing modelHourly fee per allocated RCU / WCUPay-per-request (per 1M reads/writes)Auto ScalingOptional (Target tracking scaling rules)Built-in automatic instant scalingCost optimizationCheaper for high-volume steady trafficCheaper for low-volume or unknown traffic

whyItMatters: This matters because cost optimization for predictable continuous workloads (Provisioned) vs. unpredictable/spiky workloads (On-Demand) is heavily tested on SAA-C03.
costWarning: DynamoDB capacity, storage, backup, Streams, Global Tables, and data-transfer charges may apply depending on configuration.

title: Create a DynamoDB Global Secondary Index (GSI)
goal: Goal: Add a Global Secondary Index (GSI) with an alternate partition/sort key on an existing table, select projected attributes, and execute queries against the index.

concepts.title: Global Secondary Index (GSI)
concepts.body: An index with a Partition Key and optional Sort Key that can be different from those on the base table. Can be created or deleted anytime.

concepts.title: Local Secondary Index (LSI) vs GSI
concepts.body: GSI: Alternate PK & SK; can be created anytime; uses dedicated GSI throughput. LSI: Same PK, alternate SK; MUST be created at table creation time.

concepts.title: Attribute Projections
concepts.body: Specifies which attributes are copied from the base table into the index: KEYS_ONLY, INCLUDE, or ALL.

concepts.title: GSI Consistency & Write Throttling
concepts.body: GSIs are always eventually consistent. If write capacity on a GSI is insufficient, writes to the base table will be throttled.

concepts.title: GSI vs LSI Architectural Decision Matrix
concepts.body: FeatureGlobal Secondary Index (GSI)Local Secondary Index (LSI)Partition Key (PK)Can be different from base table PKMust be SAME as base table PKCreation timeAnytime (During or after table creation)Table creation time ONLYRead consistencyEventually consistent ONLYStrongly or eventually consistentThroughput capacityDedicated RCU / WCU per indexShares base table RCU / WCUSize limitNo size limit per partition10 GB limit per partition key item collection

whyItMatters: This matters because querying non-primary key attributes without full table scans, understanding GSI eventual consistency, and managing write throughput throttling are heavily tested on SAA-C03.

title: Compare ElastiCache Redis vs Memcached
goal: Goal: Comparison breakdown focusing on multi-AZ, persistent data structures/replication (Redis) vs. simple multithreaded key-value caching (Memcached).

concepts.title: Amazon ElastiCache Overview
concepts.body: Fully managed in-memory data store service that accelerates application performance by caching frequently accessed data in RAM.

concepts.title: ElastiCache for Redis / Valkey
concepts.body: In-memory data store supporting advanced data structures (Strings, Hashes, Lists, Sets, Sorted Sets), snapshots, Multi-AZ failover, and Pub/Sub.

concepts.title: ElastiCache for Memcached
concepts.body: Pure, simple, multithreaded in-memory key-value cache designed for simple horizontal scaling without persistence or replication.

concepts.title: Persistence & Replication Comparison
concepts.body: Redis: Supports data persistence (snapshots/AOF), Multi-AZ replication, and automatic failover. Memcached: Purely volatile memory; no persistence, no replication.

title: Create an ElastiCache Cluster & Implement Caching Patterns
goal: Goal: Launch a small ElastiCache cluster inside a VPC private subnet, review connection endpoints, and evaluate Lazy Loading vs. Write-Through caching patterns.

concepts.title: ElastiCache VPC Subnet Groups
concepts.body: ElastiCache clusters should ALWAYS be deployed in private subnets with a Security Group allowing inbound port 6379 (Redis) or 11211 (Memcached) from application servers.

concepts.title: Lazy Loading (Cache-Aside Pattern)
concepts.body: App checks cache first. If hit, return data. If miss, read from RDS, write result to cache with TTL, and return data. Pros: Only requested data is cached. Cons: Cache miss penalty.

concepts.title: Write-Through Caching Pattern
concepts.body: App writes data to database and cache simultaneously. Pros: Data in cache is never stale. Cons: Write penalty; caches data that might never be read.

concepts.title: Cache Eviction & TTL
concepts.body: Setting a Time-To-Live (TTL) on cached keys prevents stale data from persisting when underlying database records are updated.

concepts.title: Caching Patterns Decision Matrix
concepts.body: Caching PatternHow It WorksProsConsPrimary Use CaseLazy Loading (Cache-Aside)App reads cache; on miss, reads DB & populates cacheNode failure is not fatal; caches only requested dataCache miss latency penalty; risk of stale data without TTLRead-heavy, general-purpose web application cachingWrite-ThroughApp writes to DB and cache simultaneouslyCache is never stale; fast subsequent readsWrite latency penalty; stores unread data in RAMFinancial systems, user profile updates, real-time inventory

whyItMatters: This matters because offloading database read pressure and reducing latency for high-traffic relational databases using Lazy Loading vs. Write-Through caching patterns is heavily tested on SAA-C03.

consoleSteps.title: Evaluate Lazy Loading (Cache-Aside) Code Pattern

instructions.text: Review Lazy Loading logic flow:
1. App queries Redis: `data = redis.get(user_id)`
2. If `data` exists (Cache Hit), return `data` immediately.
3. If `data` is null (Cache Miss), query RDS database: `data = db.query(user_id)`.
4. Save to Redis with TTL: `redis.setex(user_id, 3600, data)`.
5. Return `data` to user.

consoleSteps.note: Lazy Loading ensures only actively requested records consume cache memory.

consoleSteps.title: Evaluate Write-Through Caching Code Pattern

instructions.text: Review Write-Through logic flow:
1. App updates data: `db.update(user_id, new_data)`
2. App immediately updates Redis: `redis.set(user_id, new_data)`.
3. Subsequent reads hit Redis directly with zero chance of stale data.

consoleSteps.note: Write-Through avoids stale cache data at the cost of additional write latency.

concepts.title: Amazon Redshift Overview

concepts.title: OLAP vs OLTP

concepts.title: Columnar Storage Architecture

concepts.title: Redshift Serverless Workgroups & RPUs
